content.text:
I've had this thought on my mind for a while now. It's a story of sorts that I'd like to tell. Not necessarily because I think it's some great inspirational story that people should hear, but because I think it would be a serious challenge. Not just a challenge to my writing and storytelling skills (which are already quite dubious) but a serious thought puzzle. It falls somewhat in the realm of science fiction and philosophy. I'm going to try to write at least a short-story's worth this year in hopes of fleshing out the idea a bit more and seeing if it's truly feasible for me. The main challenge will be to find a way to tell a story that doesn't rely on the typical elements of narrative. By that I don't mean plot tropes, I mean the very essence of the human experience, the actual framework with which we understand the universe. Such elements like time, perspective, individuality, and form. To a certain extent I think of these as the basis vectors with which we construct our reality. In the common man's universe, it makes no sense to define an address by asking first what it means to have a position in space. You could always attempt to engage your next taxi driver in a debate about the merits of defining a position in any given coordinate system, but I'm not sure you'll make it to your destination on time... In mathematics however, we often do consider different coordinate systems, even different numbers of dimensions. We even ask questions about the metric that defines the transformations or mappings between our basis vectors. In physics we ask about the interplay between time and space as coordinates. At the risk of getting a bit lost in the sauce, we could go a layer higher and ask questions of directions, localization, individuality, and form all together. What would a universe without space or time look like? What about individuality? Form? I am I because I exist in a manner contiguous in both space and time. My arm is not I, for I can lose it and still exist. But all the particles that currently comprise my body, assembled in a neat pile prior to my birth, are also not I. There is something sacred about the continuity of my consciousness that preserves the concept of individuality. Or at least, the illusion of continuity.

A topic that has gripped my imagination for some time is that of the Boltzmann brain. Within the framework of our understanding of the universe it is a neat gedanken. It is exciting to imagine some random collection of particles in a dust cloud happening to condense in just such a manner to create a human brain with all of our memories and experiences for the smallest of instances. But again we somewhat compulsively impose the rules of our universe on this transient entity. Even the transient and stochastic nature of such a phenomenon is inherently defined by our framework. Why must it be rare, or transient, or exist in a universe with a flow of time at all? What are the odds that some random process would generate a Boltzmann brain? Well to that I am breathtakingly clueless, but whatever the odds are, I imagine the odds of that Boltzmann brain conjuring a world with the exact same laws of nature would be many orders of magnitude smaller yet! Perhaps causality itself is not a fundamental law. Hell, the fact that anything exists at all proves (within our current framework of logic) that causality as an assumption has failed at least once. Sometimes I dream of fantastical things that have no basis in reality. Perhaps just as well the brain could conjure a make-believe concept like time or physical form that has no basis in the universe in which it is embedded.

This is where the story descends into complete and utter chaos. The concepts evaporate just as fast as they materialize. Every new idea is met with that one question that annihilates it in search of a deeper truth. But what assumptions does that require? And what if they were untrue?

For example: I believe I am in my room typing this on my computer. But what if localization was not an element of our universe? Then perhaps I am permeating through the entire universe thinking these thoughts to myself. But what if the universe did not have any space through which one could permeate? Then I am simply existing in some ephemeral form thinking these thoughts to myself. But this implies an individuality, a separation of myself from something else. What if there existed no such way to demarcate any single thing? Then the universe itself is thinking these thoughts. But a thought is implicitly transient. To think one requires a flow of time. Without time as a tenet of reality, what becomes of thought?

One can see how this gets out of hand quite quickly. We have stripped away our laws of nature and asked what is left in their absence, but now we attempt the impossible. We now consider what new fundamental laws of reality may exist in a universe unlike our own, perhaps one our little brain has been born into. At first this seems to be a fool's errand. The very process of thinking requires and is built upon the assumptions of our reality, to generate truly orthogonal principals seems a herculean effort. Sure we could ask, what if pi was 3.15, what if time was a little slower? But these are not new degrees of freedom, these are coordinate transforms, slight adjustments to parameters that live in the same laws that we accept. We are quite literally asking to visualize a new dimension. Any physics student will be familiar with the futility of trying to visualize a higher spatial dimension. We are now attempting that with the fundamental laws of nature. The mind truly boggles.

Ok that was quite the tangent, but that's a short synopsis of the framework in which I'd like to tell a story. I imagine it will take many years to do it well. While It would be fascinating to explore what kinds of stories could be told in the absence of these fundamental laws of reality, the feat of all feats would be to tell a consistent story subject to an entirely different set.
